before.title: Conormal-node composition multiplicities under residue induction
before.statement:
In the notation of
[[thm-normal-node-composition-multiplicities-under-residue-restriction]], let
$B$ be an addable $i$-node of the $p$-restricted partition $\mu$ such that
$\nu=\mu\cup B$ is again $p$-restricted, and let $F_i$ be the residue-summand
induction functor of
[[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]]. Then
$$[\,F_iD(\mu):D(\nu)\,]=0$$
if $B$ is not a conormal $i$-node of $\mu$, and
$$[\,F_iD(\mu):D(\nu)\,]=\#\{B':\ B'\ \text{conormal }i\text{-node of }\mu\text{ weakly above }B\}$$
(counting $B$ itself) if $B$ is conormal. The dual Specht-to-induction Hom
criterion (Kleshchev survey Theorem 11.7(i), Brundan 1998 Theorem 2.5 dual
form) is a distinct statement and is not asserted here.
before.strategy: The scaffold's unshifted duality identity $[F_iD(\mu):D(\nu)]=[E_iD(\nu):D(\mu)]$ is false in characteristic $2$ and is not used. The proof records Kleshchev's survey Theorem 11.7(ii) (Brundan-Kleshchev translation functors): the multiplicity is the number of conormal $i$-nodes weakly above $B$, and $0$ otherwise; the local content is the dual-transfer discussion (induction is both a left and a right adjoint of restriction, with the antipode-invariant residue projections giving the shift), the bookkeeping of weakly-above counts against the normal-node theorem, and the characteristic-$2$ calibration $p=2$, $\mu=(1)$: $F_1D(1)\cong kS_2$ with $D(1,1)$ of multiplicity $2$, while $[E_1D(1,1):D(1)]=1$, exhibiting the failure of the naive identity. No complex-character reciprocity and no Fock-space input are used, and the dual Hom criterion is not asserted.

after.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$ of characteristic $p>0$, a $p$-restricted partition $\mu$ of $d$, an addable residue-$i$ node $B$ such that $\nu=\mu+B$ is $p$-restricted, and the actual residue induction functor $F_i$.

[F1] The actual Schur coefficient foundation and root-interval basis/count supplier holds over every field, for arbitrary dominant polynomial weights and all intervals. Negative coefficient words span, positive coefficient words detect, binary-root weight spaces have dimension $E_a(r,s)=\varepsilon_a(r,s)$, and the finite integer recurrence is $E_a(r,s)=\nu_a(r,s)+\sum_{u=r+1}^sE'_a(r,u-1)\nu_a(u,s)$, with $E'_a(r,t)=E_{a+\omega_t}(r,t)$. Its normal-stack proof includes zero coordinates and killed roots ([[lem-type-a-modular-root-interval-essential-subset-basis-and-count]]).

[F2] The proved local $q=1$ Schur/group corner in steps 14.1–15.1 of [[thm-kleshchev-first-level-branching-multiplicity]] identifies the regular Weyl corner and cell form with the Murphy cell and form, with scalar $1$, and proves equality of their radical corners. Thus $L_N(\lambda)e=D(\lambda)$ for restricted $\lambda$ and is zero otherwise; surviving labels are distinct. Its tensorword convention is explicit, and its proof uses ordinary-group survival rather than the held finite-$e$ classifier. The integral ordinary Specht basis and signed-conjugate identification are [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]] and [[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]].

[F3] On the complex ordinary Specht module, the joint Jucys–Murphy spectrum is the tableau-content spectrum ([[thm-jucys-murphy-joint-spectrum-is-the-set-of-tableau-content-vectors]]). Only its integral central operator-identity consequence is used, not any characteristic-zero composition count.

[F4] The boundary signature is read top to bottom with addable $+$, removable $-$ and cancellation $-+$ ([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). The actual primary projections define the direct residue decomposition of induction ([[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]]). Neither primitive-block classification nor an adjunction transfer of composition counts is used.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For $d>0$ take $N=d+1$, pad $\mu$ by zeros, set $a_j=\mu_j-\mu_{j+1}$, let $L=L_N(\mu)$ be the actual Schur simple, $V=F^N$, and $M=V\otimes L$. Tensor coefficient operators are the actual polynomial Schur operators of degree $d+1$, obtained by multiplying the two polynomial matrix actions. This works over finite fields without replacing coefficient actions by evaluated group elements. The case $d=0$ is treated below. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Here is the local component identity used below. If a binary root deficit has separated connected components (a zero simple-root coefficient between consecutive components), its negative words split into products supported on those components. All cross-component positive and negative root operators commute, and their Cartan characters on the other component are unchanged: their simple-root supports are nonadjacent. Move the positive words past the other components and evaluate their highest coefficients one component at a time. The positive/negative coefficient matrix is consequently the tensor product of the component matrices. Negative-word spanning and positive detection identify its quotient by the common positive-test kernel with the actual simple weight space. Hence this weight space is the tensor product of the component quotients, including when one is zero. This proves the assertion directly from coefficient words; it does not assume a tensor-product decomposition of the whole simple module. [step 1.1, F1, F2, construct]

3.1 In particular fix one component $\delta$. Choose a negative basis $f_1v,\ldots,f_tv$ of its quotient and positive tests $e_1,\ldots,e_t$ dual to it. They are finite linear combinations of actual coefficient words, with coefficients in $F$; their existence follows from positive detection and ordinary finite-dimensional linear algebra. Then $P_\delta=\sum_{h=1}^t f_he_h$ is the identity on every binary weight space having this component and any separated other components. The same tests apply because the other components change none of the Cartan data of $\delta$. If $t=0$, these weight spaces are zero. This is an identity of coefficient operators on those spaces, so it descends to subquotients. [step 2.1, F1, F2, construct]

4.1 Write $\xi_i=\mu+\epsilon_i$. Suppose a simple composition factor with highest weight $\eta$ contributes at $\xi_i$. All weights of $M$ are at most $\mu+\epsilon_1$, and weights of that factor are at most $\eta$. Thus $\xi_i\le\eta\le\mu+\epsilon_1.$ [step 3.1, F1, F2, construct]

5.1 The deficit $\Gamma=\mu+\epsilon_1-\eta$ has simple-root coefficients $0$ or $1$ in positions $1,\ldots,i-1$ and zero elsewhere. On a tensor summand $v_j\otimes L_{\eta-\epsilon_j}$ the deficit in $L$ is $\Gamma-(\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_{j-1}).$ [step 4.1, F1, F2, construct]

6.1 It must be nonnegative. Consequently every possible label $j$ lies before the first missing coefficient in $\Gamma$. If $\Gamma$ has a component $\delta$ after that first gap, every positive or negative coefficient word supported on $\delta$ fixes the $V$ factor (its nonconstant terms annihilate each of these labels). Its action on this tensor weight is therefore purely its action on $L$. The preceding $P_\delta$ is the identity on the entire weight $M_\eta$, not just on individual tensor summands. [step 5.1, F1, F2, construct]

7.1 Choose a composition series and a lift $x\in M_\eta$ of the nonzero highest vector of the proposed factor in its series quotient. Each $e_hx$ lies in the preceding submodule because it has strictly higher weight, and each $f_h$ preserves that submodule. But $P_\delta x=x$ would then place $x$ in it, a contradiction. If the component quotient is zero there was no such tensor weight to start with. Thus $\Gamma$ has no later component. Its only possible nonzero coefficients form one initial interval, and $\eta=\mu+\epsilon_u\quad\text{for some }u\le i.$ [step 6.1, F1, F2, construct]

8.1 This excludes only highest weights of factors contributing to $\xi_i$. It asserts nothing about distant tensor factors. [step 7.1, F1, F2, construct]

9.1 Since every weight of $L$ is at most $\mu$, $M_{\xi_i}=\bigoplus_{j\le i}v_j\otimes L_{\mu+\epsilon_i-\epsilon_j},\qquad d_i:=\dim M_{\xi_i}=1+\sum_{j<i}E_a(j,i-1).$ [step 8.1, F1, F2, construct]

10.1 Let $b_u$ be the actual composition multiplicity of $L_N(\mu+\epsilon_u)$ in $M$ when that weight is dominant; set $b_u=0$ otherwise. No restrictedness condition is imposed on these auxiliary factors. The support lemma and the one-dimensional highest spaces give $d_i=b_i+\sum_{u<i}b_uE_{a+\omega_u}(u,i-1).$ (equation C). [step 9.1, F1, F2, construct]

11.1 Indeed $\mu+\epsilon_u-\xi_i=\alpha_u+\cdots+\alpha_{i-1}$. On this interval the fundamental coordinates of the dominant weight $\mu+\epsilon_u$ are those of $a$ with its first coordinate $u$ increased by one; the coordinate $u-1$ changed by minus one lies outside the interval. Nondominant rows have multiplicity zero, so their formal summands cause no alteration of (C). [step 10.1, F1, F2, construct]

12.1 For completeness the weight-dimension symmetry needed here is local. Permutation matrices permute the integer weight spaces of $L$. Hence its lowest weight is $w_0\mu$, its space is one dimensional, and every weight lies between $w_0\mu$ and $\mu$. The contragredient dual twisted by $\det^d$ is a polynomial simple of highest weight $\mu^*=(d-\mu_N,\ldots,d-\mu_1).$ [step 11.1, F1, F2, construct]

13.1 One can verify polynomiality without a rational-module classification theorem. The tensorword Schur algebra acts faithfully on $V^{\otimes d}$; its regular module embeds in a finite direct sum of copies of this tensor space by its action on a basis. Thus every simple is a subquotient of copies of this tensor space. Duality and the twist make it a subquotient of $(V^*\otimes\det)^{\otimes d}$; the explicit exterior-complement pairing gives $V^*\otimes\det\cong\bigwedge^{N-1}V$ over every field. It is therefore polynomial. Positive and negative coefficients interchange under duality, so the highest weight just identified determines the same actual Schur simple as in the accepted foundation. These statements are coefficient identities; over a finite field they can equivalently be checked over $F(t)$ and descended as the identical finite matrices. [step 12.1, F1, F2, construct]

14.1 Put $\bar a_t=a_{N-t}$. Duality reverses roots and preserves weight dimensions, yielding $E_a(j,i-1)=E_{\bar a}(N-i+1,N-j).$ [step 13.1, F1, F2, construct]

15.1 This argument applies also to any dominant shifted weight. In particular the first-coordinate shift at $u$ becomes the final-coordinate shift at $N-u$ on the reversed interval. No restriction on its fundamental coordinates is needed. [step 14.1, F1, F2, construct]

16.1 Reverse the indices: $r=N-i+1$, $\bar b_r=b_i$, $\bar d_r=d_i$. On indices $1,\ldots,N$, let the strictly upper triangular matrices be $A[r,v]=\nu'_{\bar a}(r,v-1),\qquad B[r,v]=E'_{\bar a}(r,v-1)\quad(r<v).$ [step 15.1, F1, construct]

17.1 For $r<v$, apply the accepted recurrence to $[r,v-1]$ after increasing coordinate $v-1$. Every earlier interval $[r,u-1]$ with $u<v$ is unaffected, while the tail normal count is shifted at $v-1$. Thus $B[r,v]=A[r,v]+\sum_{r<u<v}B[r,u]A[u,v]$, or $B=A+BA$. Hence $(I+B)(I-A)=I$. Since these are finite integer matrices, the inverse is two-sided and $(I+B)^{-1}=I-A$. Equivalently, the supplier's first-cut recurrence gives $B=A+AB$ and $I+B=I+A+\cdots+A^{N-1}$. [step 16.1, F1, construct]

18.1 Let $H_r=\sum_{s=r}^{N-1}\nu_{\bar a}(r,s)$, with $H_N=0$. Applying the accepted recurrence separately for every endpoint and summing gives $\bar d=\mathbf1+(I+B)H.$ [step 17.1, F1, construct]

19.1 Opposition turns (C) into $\bar d=(I+B)\bar b$. Multiplication by $I-A$ gives, as ordinary integers, $b_i=1+\sum_{s=r}^{N-1}\bigl(\nu_{\bar a}(r,s)-\nu'_{\bar a}(r,s)\bigr),\qquad r=N-i+1.$ (equation D). [step 18.1, F1, construct]

20.1 This is finite nilpotent matrix arithmetic. It neither divides in $F$ nor replaces a composition multiplicity by a residue in $F$. [step 19.1, F1, construct]

21.1 Use the accepted normal-stack interpretation; every coordinate and $B,C$ equality tested in this paragraph and the endpoint analysis is modulo $p$, whereas stack heights are ordinary integers. Write $\sigma(r,t)$ for its alive indicator and put $\sigma(r,r-1)=1$. For every dominant coordinate array $\lambda$, $\nu_\lambda(r,s)-\nu'_\lambda(r,s)=\sigma(r,s-1)\left(\mathbf1_{B(r,s)=-1}-\mathbf1_{B(r,s)=0}\right).$ (equation E). [step 20.1, F1, construct]

22.1 If killed before the final step, both counts are zero. Otherwise let its current height be $h\ge1$. The endpoint shift keeps $C(r,s)$ fixed and replaces $B$ and $\lambda_s$ by $B+1$ and $\lambda_s+1$. If $B=-1$ it creates a pop and lowers the count by one; when $\lambda_s=-1$, the unshifted step instead pushes and the shifted zero-coordinate step is neutral, with the same difference. If $B=0$ it removes a pop and increases the count by one; when $\lambda_s=0$, the old step is neutral and the new step pushes, again with that difference. For other $B$ neither change alters the count. If a pop removes the initial root, its new count is zero, still $h-1=0$. At $s=r$ the two counts are $\mathbf1_{\lambda_r\ne0}$ and $\mathbf1_{\lambda_r+1\ne0}$, giving the same formula. These alternatives are exhaustive and valid for $p=2$. [step 21.1, F1, construct]

23.1 Fix an actual addable row $i$ and put $R_j=\mu_j+1-j$, $\rho=R_i\pmod p$. If $i>1$, addability means $a_{i-1}>0$. Since $\mu$ is restricted, $0<a_{i-1}<p$; the reversed root therefore starts alive. For $r=N-i+1$, $s=N-j$, direct substitution gives $B_{\bar a}(r,s)=R_j-R_i-1,\qquad C_{\bar a}(r,s)=R_{j+1}-R_i.$ [step 22.1, F1, F4, construct]

24.1 Thus the two indicators in (E) respectively detect an addable-position residue $\rho$ in row $j$ and a removable-position residue $\rho$ in row $j$. The normal stack processes the boundary in reverse order, starting with the chosen $+$ in row $i$. At step $j$ its $C=0$ push corresponds to the plus in row $j+1$, and its $B=0$ pop to the minus in row $j$. The top-row plus is a pending final event. This reversal is exactly the stack evaluation of $-+$ cancellation: in a reverse scan, a minus cancels the most recently encountered plus. [step 23.1, F1, F4, construct]

25.1 Here is the precise check at flat row blocks and at the endpoints. Let $D_s=1+\sum_{t=r}^s\sigma(r,t-1)\left(\mathbf1_{B(r,t)=-1}-\mathbf1_{B(r,t)=0}\right).$ [step 24.1, F1, F4, construct]

26.1 While the chosen root remains alive, $D_s$ is its current normal-stack height plus the pending indicator $\mathbf1_{R_j=R_i}$, where $j=N-s$. At the initial step the removable event $B(r,r)=0$ cannot occur since $0<a_{i-1}<p$, and this identity follows immediately. At each subsequent live step the change in height is $\mathbf1_{C(r,s)=0}-\mathbf1_{B(r,s)=0}.$ [step 25.1, F1, F4, construct]

27.1 For $a_j\ne0$ these are disjoint push/pop events. For $a_j=0$ the indicators are equal and the step is neutral, as required by the actual stack. Subtracting this height change from the change in $D_s$ gives $\mathbf1_{R_j=R_i}-\mathbf1_{R_{j+1}=R_i},$ [step 26.1, F1, F4, construct]

28.1 which replaces the previous pending indicator by the next. This proves the invariant by induction, including flat blocks. Equivalently, at each flat boundary $a_j=0$, the virtual removable sign in row $j$ and virtual addable sign in row $j+1$ have the same residue and form an adjacent $-+$ pair in the selected-residue row-boundary word. Deleting these pairs restores exactly the actual boundary word. By signature confluence their insertion or deletion has no effect on the surviving actual nodes. The chosen node is an actual addable, so it is never among the virtual pairs. [step 27.1, F1, F4, construct]

29.1 If the initial root is killed, its preceding height was one, the current event is $B=0$, and $B=-1$ is false. The pending indicator after the step is zero. Thus $D_s=0$, and every later term is zero because the alive indicator remains zero. In the reversed boundary scan, killing the initial plus likewise means that the chosen node is canceled; later pluses above it cannot revive it. At the last step the pending indicator is the actual addable top-row plus. We have therefore evaluated exactly the reverse scan of the prefix ending at the chosen node. A minus below this prefix cannot cancel a plus in it under top-to-bottom $-+$ cancellation; the conormal decisions for this prefix agree with those in the entire signature. [step 28.1, F1, F4, construct]

30.1 Consequently (D) is zero precisely when the chosen plus is canceled. If it survives, (D) is the number of surviving pluses of residue $\rho$ in the prefix, namely the number of conormal nodes weakly above $B$. For $i=1$, (D) is $b_1=1$: the top plus survives and it is the only node weakly above itself. For completeness, a nondominant row $i>1$ has $a_{i-1}=0$; the first endpoint difference is $-1$, killing the virtual initial unit and all later differences, so (D) gives zero as required by (C). These rows were not silently discarded during the integer inversion. [step 29.1, F1, F4, construct]

31.1 Let $\omega=(1^N)$ be the regular degree-$N$ weight. Then $M_\omega=\bigoplus_{j=1}^N v_j\otimes L_{\omega-\epsilon_j}.$ [step 30.1, F2, construct]

32.1 Let $G=\mathfrak S_N$, $H=\mathfrak S_d$ fixing label $N$, and $W=L_{\omega-\epsilon_N}$. The accepted local $q=1$ corner/form calculation applies to degree $d$ and rank $N$ with regular weight $(1^d,0)$: its surviving semistandard indices are precisely standard tableaux, and evaluating the corner at $1$ gives the same Murphy basis and scalar-$1$ form, regardless of the unused last label. Its radical-corner equality therefore makes $W$ the left group module $D(\mu)$. To fix the action convention, the supplier's right corner element $\rho_h$ permutes tensorword labels by $h^{-1}$; star conversion makes left $g$ act by right $g^{-1}$, hence by label permutation $g$. The same conversion in the degree-$N$ corner gives the output action. Thus the output regular-corner action is ordinary permutation of labels: on tensorwords the corresponding orbit matrix is exactly that label permutation. Since these are identities in the actual tensorword Schur algebra, the same equality holds on $M$; it does not depend on evaluated permutation matrices spanning the Schur algebra. [step 31.1, F2, construct]

33.1 The explicit map $F[G]\otimes_{F[H]}W\longrightarrow M_\omega,\qquad g\otimes w\longmapsto g(v_N\otimes w)$. [step 32.1, F2, construct]

34.1 is well defined and $G$-equivariant. Left cosets of $H$ correspond to the image label $gN$, and their summands map bijectively to the displayed summands of $M_\omega$. It is therefore an isomorphism. This proves $M_\omega\cong\operatorname{Ind}_{\mathfrak S_d}^{\mathfrak S_{d+1}}D(\mu)$, without Frobenius reciprocity or an adjunction multiplicity assertion. [step 33.1, F2, construct]

35.1 Corner projection is exact. Each Schur composition factor $L_N(\eta)$ projects to the distinct restricted group simple $D(\eta)$ if $\eta$ is restricted, and to zero otherwise, by the accepted local form/radical and ordinary-group survival proof. Hence for a restricted $\mu+B=\mu+\epsilon_i$, its total induction multiplicity is exactly $b_i$. Nonrestricted near factors were kept until this exact projection. Distant factors were never excluded; distinct surviving labels ensure that they cannot change this particular count. When $d=0$, the single degree-one tensor/corner gives the unique plus and multiplicity one directly. [step 34.1, F2, construct]

36.1 The generalized Jucys--Murphy induction summands give a direct decomposition of total induction. For the ordinary group elements $L_k=\sum_{j<k}(j,k)$, induction by inserting the letter $n$ into a cycle gives the integral identity $\prod_{k=1}^n(t+L_k)=\sum_{g\in\mathfrak S_n}t^{\#\operatorname{cycles}(g)}g.$ [step 35.1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

37.1 The factor $t$ makes $n$ a new fixed point; each transposition $(j,n)$ inserts $n$ at the uniquely specified place in the cycle containing $j$. These alternatives are disjoint and exhaust the permutations. Coefficients on the right are class sums, so all coefficients of $Q_n(t)=\prod_{k=1}^n(t-L_k)$ are central over the integers and every field. [step 36.1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

38.1 The published [[thm-jucys-murphy-joint-spectrum-is-the-set-of-tableau-content-vectors]] says that $Q_n(t)$ acts on the complex ordinary Specht module of shape $\lambda$ as $\prod_{A\in\lambda}(t-\operatorname{res}_{\mathbb Z}(A))$. The ordinary integral Specht lattice has the free polytabloid basis provided by the accepted integral bridge. The operator equality has integer matrices on that lattice; its validity after scalar extension to $\mathbb C$ therefore implies its validity over $\mathbb Z$. Reducing and taking its radical quotient proves the same content scalar on ordinary $D^\lambda$ over every field. The accepted signed-conjugate dictionary sends each $L_k$ to $-L_k$ under the sign twist, and transpose negates contents. Hence $Q_n(t)$ acts on restricted $D(\lambda)=D^{\lambda'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ by the content polynomial of $\lambda$. This use of the published complex spectrum is an integral operator-identity descent; none of the multiplicity inversion uses characteristic-zero composition counts or semisimplicity. [step 37.1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

39.1 Let $\alpha$ be the multiset of residues of $\mu$. The exact central content polynomial on $D(\mu)$ and the central CRT description of the content sums give $e_\alpha^{(d)}D(\mu)=D(\mu)$; this requires no primitive-block assertion. For clarity the functor idempotent $e=e_\alpha^{(d)}P_{d+1,h}$ implies the following test on $F_hD(\mu)=F\mathfrak S_{d+1}e\otimes_{F\mathfrak S_d}D(\mu)$. On its generating subspace $e\otimes D(\mu)$, the first-$d$ content polynomial has exactly the scalar for $\mu$, and $L_{d+1}-h$ is nilpotent. These operators commute and $(L_{d+1}-h)^m e=0$ for a fixed primary exponent $m$. A coefficient $z$ of $Q_{d+1}(t)-(t-h)Q_\mu(t)$ is central by the integral identity. On $e\otimes w$ it is the corresponding scalar coefficient of $Q_\mu(t)$ times $h-L_{d+1}$: balance the first-$d$ central coefficient across $e$ into $w$. Centrality lets this same calculation iterate, so $z^m(e\otimes w)=0$. Since the whole module is generated by these vectors and $z$ commutes with every group translate, $z^m$ is zero on the whole module. On a simple factor a nilpotent central endomorphism is zero, since every nonzero simple-module endomorphism is invertible. Thus every factor in this summand has content polynomial $(t-h)Q_\mu(t)$. [step 38.1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

40.1 Distinct residues give distinct polynomials: $(t-h)Q_\mu(t)-(t-k)Q_\mu(t)=(k-h)Q_\mu(t)\ne0$ for $h\ne k$. The content polynomial of $\mu+B$ appends exactly the residue of $B$. Its factors therefore occur only in the corresponding residue summand. The total multiplicity computed above is exactly the multiplicity in $F_iD(\mu)$ required by the target. This argument does not use primitivity or exhaustiveness of any content-block idempotent. [step 39.1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

41.1 Transpose preserves boundary types. Literally $(\mu\cup B)'=\mu'\cup B^{\mathsf t},\qquad(\mu\setminus A)'=\mu'\setminus A^{\mathsf t}.$ [step 40.1, F4, construct]

42.1 It sends an addable node to an addable node and a removable node to a removable node; it negates the residue. The appropriate boundary reading order is reversed when transporting the signature convention. It does not exchange addable and removable sets. The proof above needs no claimed equality of induction and restriction multiplicities and no transpose transfer of a restriction count. [step 41.1, F4, construct]

43.1 The finite character inversion, boundary-stack calculation, exact induction corner and residue allocation just proved identify the stated multiplicity with zero off conormality and with the conormal weak-above count on conormality. Both cases hold over every field of characteristic $p$, with nonrestricted auxiliary factors retained until projection and no assertion about other tensor factors. [step 42.1, F1, F2, F4, construct] ∎

## Remarks

The survey documents the formula's origin; its count is not a proof premise. Biadjunction does not equate these composition multiplicities: in characteristic $2$, induction of $D(1)$ to $S_2$ has multiplicity $2$ of $D(1,1)$, whereas restricting that simple has multiplicity $1$ of $D(1)$. The proof instead uses actual tensor weights, finite integer inversion and an explicit coset map.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 We first establish the restriction endpoint locally. Work with left Schur modules through star. In tensor degree $m$, the word of $m_\alpha T_w$ has $j$th letter the row containing $j$ in $t^\alpha w$; at regular type it is $jw^{-1}$, with zero-multiplicity labels omitted. Over $K=F(t)$ the evaluations $g^{\otimes m}$ span the tensor Schur algebra: a functional killing them gives a polynomial zero on invertible matrices; multiplication by $\det$ and the infinite-field polynomial identity force that polynomial to be zero. Schur simples are therefore simple polynomial $\mathrm{GL}_N$ modules. The canonical shape/type diagonal is its permutation-summand projection, whose square gives canonical form value one. Semistandard column strictness bounds entries at most $k$ by the first $k$ rows, so all weights are dominated by the highest weight $\xi$ and the highest space is $Kv$. Integer torus characters, rather than Lie eigenvalues modulo $p$, distinguish these weights. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Gaussian factorization $g=u^-tu^+$ on the big cell shows that negative coefficient operators on $v$ span its simple module: a functional killing them kills $gv$ on that open set and hence everywhere by polynomial identity. Similarly, positive coefficient operators detect every nonzero vector $x$ of weight $\xi-\Gamma$. If every positive highest coefficient vanished, the highest coefficient of $gx$ would vanish on the big cell, because negative operators cannot raise any weight to $\xi$; it would then vanish on the orbit of $x$, which spans the simple and contains $v$. All coefficient operators have integral tensor replacement matrices, and the ranks and Hom kernels of finite matrices preserve extension from $F$ to $K$. These arguments consequently descend to $F$. [step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Let $\xi_N=0$, $l=N-1$, and let $M$ be the full last-coordinate-one subspace of $L_N(\xi)$. A primitive vector means one killed by every nonconstant coefficient of the upper Levi unipotent group, not merely by its Lie generators. Factor the full upper group as $V U_l^+$, where $V$ has only the last column above the diagonal nontrivial. A positive test of a Levi-primitive vector acts only through $V$, since the right-hand nonconstant Levi coefficients kill it. Raising last coordinate $1$ to highest coordinate $0$ requires a $V$ monomial of degree exactly one. Positive detection therefore gives $E_{rN}x=cv\ne0$ for some $r$. Hence $\operatorname{wt}(x)=\xi-\beta_r$, where $\beta_r=\alpha_r+\cdots+\alpha_l$, even when the initial first-level deficit was arbitrary. On that primitive weight space $x\mapsto E_{rN}x$ is injective by the same detection argument, so its dimension is at most one. [step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Put $a_j=\xi_j-\xi_{j+1}$ and use $B(r,s)=s-r+\sum_{j=r}^s a_j$ and $C(r,s)=s-r+\sum_{j=r}^{s-1}a_j$. For nonempty $I$, the canonical $Q(I)$ kills a primitive vector: if $b=\min I$, its ascending-prefix letter $e_{b-1}$ commutes past the remaining ascending letters, whose indices exceed $b$, and becomes a rightmost Levi letter with $b-1<l$. Expand a nonzero primitive vector of weight $\xi-\beta_r$ in the essential $T$ basis and select the largest hat among its nonzero coefficients. The triangular pivot isolates a nonzero term. That hat cannot be nonempty, since its $Q$ test would annihilate the vector. Distinct essential hats therefore leave exactly one essential set with empty hat. Empty is linked precisely to a regular set, and the essential-regular matching theorem says such a set exists precisely when $r$ is normal. This proves necessity of normality. [step 3.1, F2, construct]

5.1 Conversely, for normal $r$ let $R_r=\{s\in(r,l]:B(r,s)=0\}$ and choose its compensation $f$ with $r<f(s)\le s$ and $B(f(s),s)=0$. Put $D=f(R_r)$. 6.1 We separate primitive labels integrally, including $p=2$. before.title: Separated Hecke residues give seminormal idempotents and bases
before.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, let $e=e(F,q)$ and assume $e>n$ (with $e=\infty$ allowed); let $\lambda\vdash n$, $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$, and let $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ be the Murphy cell module with Murphy basis $(m_t)_{t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).
1. (**Separation**) If $s,t$ are standard $\lambda$-tableaux with $[\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q$ for all $1\le k\le n$ then $s=t$. More precisely, if the q-content values agree for all $k\notin\{i,i+1\}$ for some $i$, then $s=t$ or $t=s(i\ i+1)$.
2. (**Idempotents**) For a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ define, inside the commutative algebra $F[L_1,\dots,L_n]$, $$F_t:=\prod_{k=1}^{n}\ \prod_{\substack{s\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\\[\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q\ne[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q}}\frac{L_k-[\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q}{[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q-[\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q}$$ and put $f_t:=m_tF_t\in S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$. All denominators are nonzero by (1) and the $f_t$ are well-defined spectral projectors: $f_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q\,f_t$, and $f_t=m_t+\sum_{s\rhd t}a_sm_s$ for suitable $a_s\in F$.
3. (**Orthogonal seminormal basis**) $\{f_t:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is a basis of $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ satisfying $f_tF_s=\delta_{ts}f_t$ and $\langle f_s,f_t\rangle_\lambda=\delta_{st}\langle f_t,f_t\rangle_\lambda$; it is the **seminormal basis** of the Murphy cell module.
4. (**Generator action**) Let $s$ be a standard $\lambda$-tableau, $1\le i<n$ and $t:=s(i\ i+1)$, and put $\rho:=\operatorname{content}_s(i)-\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)\in\mathbb Z$ (an integer; it equals $\operatorname{res}_s(i)-\operatorname{res}_t(i)$ in the source's notation). If $i$ and $i+1$ lie in the same row of $s$ then $f_sT_i=q\,f_s$; if they lie in the same column then $f_sT_i=-f_s$; otherwise $t$ is standard and $$f_sT_i=\alpha_i(s)\,f_t-\frac{1}{[\rho]_q}f_s,\qquad \alpha_i(s):=\begin{cases}1,&s\rhd t,\\[1mm]\dfrac{[1+\rho]_q[1-\rho]_q}{[\rho]_q[-\rho]_q},&t\rhd s,\end{cases}$$ where $[-\rho]_q$ is the extended quantum integer of [[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]] and for the swapped tableau $\operatorname{content}_t(i)-\operatorname{content}_t(i+1)=-\rho$. No semisimplicity of $H$ is assumed and no choice principle is used.

after.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e>n$, a partition $\lambda\vdash n$, the Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ with Murphy basis $(m_t)$ and cell form ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]), and the q-content values of [[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]].

[F1] ([[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]]) $m_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q\,m_t+\sum_{v\rhd t}a_vm_v$ in $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$; the $L_k$ commute pairwise and every symmetric polynomial in them is central.

[F2] ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]) For $e>n$ no $m$ with $1\le m\le n$ has $[m]_q=0$; more precisely, if two integer contents $c,c'$ with $|c-c'|\le n$ satisfy $[c]_q=[c']_q$ then $c=c'$.

[F3] ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) The cell form on $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is symmetric and associative, and the star anti-involution fixes each $L_k$; the Murphy basis is triangular along the dominance order on tableaux.

[F4] Source results: separation of q-content sequences for $e>n$ and the seminormal spectral construction are Mathas, Lemma 3.32, Proposition 3.33 and Theorem 3.34 (printed pp. 30-34); the coefficient system of part 4 as displayed is that of Hu-Mathas, Example 3.11 with the axial distance (3.8), Lemma 3.12 and Proposition 3.17, the 1998 manuscript's $t\rhd s$ branch being inconsistent with the Hecke relations. The abstract form of the spectral construction under the separation condition is Mathas, Proposition 4.13 with the appendix.





## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Reconstruct a tableau from its residue tuple. At a prefix of size $k-1$, two different addable corners have integer content difference of absolute value at most $k$. Since $[a]_q-[b]_q=q^b[a-b]_q$ and $e>n$, their q-contents differ. Starting with the empty diagram, the tuple thus recovers each added node and the final shape. For two tableaux of a fixed shape with identical entries' residues outside $i,i+1$, first reconstruct the common prefix through $i-1$, and reconstruct the common suffix by successively deleting the unique appropriate removable corner from the fixed final shape. The intervening skew diagram has two boxes; its only possible orders are the original order and its swap. This proves both separation assertions. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 Diagonalize the commuting JM operators on a cell. Their triangular basis gives a filtration with one-dimensional joint characters indexed by standard tableaux. Those characters are distinct by step 1.1. For commuting triangular operators, the simultaneous generalized eigenspaces split along their distinct joint characters: the corresponding maximal ideals of the polynomial algebra are pairwise comaximal. Each joint character occurs once in this cell, so each generalized eigenspace is one-dimensional and hence an actual joint eigenline. This finite Chinese-remainder argument works over any field and needs no choice of a generic scalar or algebraic closure. The Lagrange product of the Statement is $1$ on its target tuple and $0$ on every other tuple. Applied to $m_t$, its triangular diagonal coefficient is $1$, and the other possible terms are strictly more dominant. Thus it gives the asserted $f_t$. [F1, step 1.1]

2.2 Compute the diagonal coefficient using the **correctly ordered** JM relation $$T_iL_i=L_{i+1}T_i-(q-1)L_{i+1}-1.$$ For $k\ne i,i+1$, $T_i$ commutes with $L_k$. Consequently separation restricts $f_sT_i$ to the span of $f_s$ and $f_t$ if the swap is standard, or to $f_s$ alone otherwise. Write its coefficient of $f_s$ as $c_s$. The displayed relation gives $$c_s\bigl([\operatorname{content}_s(i)]_q-              [\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)]_q\bigr)    =-(q-1)[\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)]_q-1.$$ Its denominator is $q^{\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)}[\rho]_q$, while the numerator is $-q^{\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)}$, so $c_s=-1/[\rho]_q$. This does not claim that $T_i$ commutes with $L_i$. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 At this stage step 2.1 establishes the projector identities on each individual cell module. The global identities in $H$ will follow below after proving that the sum of the cell modules is faithful. No finite-$e$ classification is a premise. [step 2.1]

3.2 The transition from $m_t$ to $f_t$ is unitriangular, so these vectors form a basis. For $s\ne t$, choose $k$ at which their q-contents differ. Self-adjointness $L_k^*=L_k$ and associativity give $$([\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q-    [\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q)\langle f_s,f_t\rangle=0.$$ The scalar is nonzero, proving orthogonality. The Lagrange action also gives $f_tF_s=\delta_{ts}f_t$. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1]

3.3 If the swap is not standard, the consecutive entries lie adjacently in one row or one column. Then $\rho=-1$ or $\rho=1$, respectively, and step 2.2 gives $c_s=q$ or $c_s=-1$. These are the stated row and column cases; the row action is $q$, not the scalar $1$ at a general parameter. [step 2.2]

4.1 Suppose the swap is standard. In the branch $s\rhd t$, the length-additive Murphy action has leading term $m_sT_i=m_t$; the unitriangular eigenbasis change then gives the off-diagonal coefficient $\alpha_i(s)=1$. Higher-dominance terms cannot alter the coefficient at $t$ in this two-dimensional eigenline span. This is the leading-term argument in the full proof of Mathas Theorem 3.34. In both branches the quadratic relation gives $$\alpha_i(s)\alpha_i(t)=q+(q-1)c_s-c_s^2  =\frac{[1+\rho]_q[1-\rho]_q}{[\rho]_q[-\rho]_q}.$$ The last equality follows directly from $[-\rho]_q=-q^{-\rho}[\rho]_q$ and the quantum-integer addition identities. Thus the opposite branch has exactly the displayed coefficient. This proves the generator formula without accepting the inconsistent branch in the 1998 manuscript. [step 3.2, step 2.2]

5.1 Prove nondegeneracy in the separated range locally. The canonical Murphy basis vector has form value $[\lambda]!_q=\prod_a[\lambda_a]!_q$, because $x_\lambda^2=[\lambda]!_qx_\lambda$; its seminormal image has the same value since the canonical tableau is dominance-maximal. This scalar is nonzero when $e>n$. If $s\rhd t=s(i,i+1)$ is a standard swap, put $a=1/[\rho]_q$. Step 4.1 gives $f_t=f_s(T_i+a)$. Associativity, orthogonality and the quadratic relation give $\langle f_t,f_t\rangle=(q+a)(1-a)\langle f_s,f_s\rangle=q[\rho+1]_q[\rho-1]_q[\rho]_q^{-2}\langle f_s,f_s\rangle$. Indeed expansion of $(T_i+a)^2$ and its $f_s$ coefficient $-a$ gives $q-a(q-1)-a^2=(q+a)(1-a)$. The swapped incomparable boxes have $2\le|\rho|\le n-1$: their row and column separations plus one are at most the size of the diagram. Thus all three quantum integers here are nonzero. Every standard tableau is connected to the canonical one by length-increasing swaps of adjacent incomparable entries: bubble-sort its linear extension of the box-order poset into the canonical row-order extension, then reverse the swaps. Induction gives nonzero diagonal norm at every $f_t$, so each cell form is nonsingular. [F2, F3, step 3.2, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Each cell is now its nonzero simple form quotient, absolutely simple, and all these cells are pairwise distinct and exhaust the simple modules by [[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]. Thus the split semisimple quotient $H/J(H)$ has dimension $\sum_\lambda |\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|^2$. This equals $\dim H$ because the Murphy cellular basis has exactly one element for each pair of standard tableaux of the same shape ([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]]). Hence $J(H)=0$, $H$ is split semisimple, and the direct sum of all its simple cell modules is faithful. On that faithful module the global Lagrange products of the Statement are the orthogonal projectors from step 2.1, with different shapes having disjoint tuples by step 1.1. Therefore $F_sF_t=\delta_{st}F_t$ holds in $H$ itself, proving the global idempotents. This argument proves only the separated range and does not assert a finite-$e$ nonzero-label criterion when $e\le n$. [step 5.1, step 2.1, step 1.1, algebra]

7.1 Steps 1.1-6.1 prove all four claims. No semisimplicity was imposed as a hypothesis: it was derived locally from nondegenerate cells and their complete finite-cell classification. The calculation concerns the intrinsic Murphy cell and keeps the signed ordinary-module dictionary separate. All products and basis changes are finite, and no choice principle is used. [step 1.1, step 3.2, step 4.1, step 6.1] ∎

before.title: Residue sequences need not separate when e is at most n
before.statement: The hypothesis $e>n$ in [[thm-separated-hecke-residues-give-seminormal-idempotents-and-bases]] cannot be dropped. Take $F=\mathbb C$, $q=-1$ (so $e=e(\mathbb C,-1)=2$, [[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), $n=3$ and $\lambda=(2,1)$. The two distinct standard tableaux $s=\begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\3\end{smallmatrix}$ and $t=\begin{smallmatrix}1&3\\2\end{smallmatrix}$ have contents $\operatorname{content}_s(1),\operatorname{content}_s(2),\operatorname{content}_s(3)=0,1,-1$ and $\operatorname{content}_t(1),\operatorname{content}_t(2),\operatorname{content}_t(3)=0,-1,1$, and since $[m]_{-1}=[m]+(-1)^{m-1}[1]_{-1}$ reduces modulo $e=2$ one has $[1]_{-1}=1=[-1]_{-1}$ ([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]] for the extended quantum integers). Hence $$([\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q)_{k=1,2,3}=(0,1,1)=([\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q)_{k=1,2,3}\quad(q=-1):$$ the q-content sequences collide although $s\ne t$, so the separation conclusion of the theorem fails. Moreover the interpolation denominator for $k=2$ is the difference $[\operatorname{content}_t(2)]_q-[\operatorname{content}_s(2)]_q=[-1]_{-1}-[1]_{-1}=0$, so the projector $F_t$ of the theorem is not defined in this case; the same collision $\rho\equiv0\bmod e$ makes $[\rho]_q=0$ in the generator formula of the theorem's part 4. Consequently no seminormal basis is available beyond the semisimple range, and the theorem's hypothesis $e>n$ is optimal.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field $\mathbb C$, $q=-1\in\mathbb C^{\times}$, $n=3$, the standard tableaux $s,t$ of shape $(2,1)$ above, and the q-integers of [[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]].

## Counterexample

1.1 Contents of the two tableaux: for $s$ with rows $(1,2)$ and $(3)$ the nodes are $(1,1),(1,2),(2,1)$ for $1,2,3$, giving contents $0,1,-1$; for $t$ with rows $(1,3)$ and $(2)$ the nodes are $(1,1),(2,1),(1,2)$ for $1,2,3$, giving contents $0,-1,1$. [given]

2.1 Collision: by [F1] and [F2], $[2]_{-1}=0$ and $[1]_{-1}=[-1]_{-1}=1$; hence $[\operatorname{content}_s(1)]_{q}=0=[\operatorname{content}_t(1)]_q$, $[\operatorname{content}_s(2)]_q=1=[\operatorname{content}_t(2)]_q$ and $[\operatorname{content}_s(3)]_q=1=[\operatorname{content}_t(3)]_q$, so the two q-content sequences coincide even though $s\ne t$. [step 1.1, F1, F2]

3.1 Interpolation and axial distance. The eigenvalue difference that would be needed to distinguish $s$ and $t$ at $k=2$ is $1-1=0$. Equal-value exclusion in a polynomial product does not make its literal denominators zero; it instead loses the factor that could distinguish these tuples. No polynomial in the JM operators can provide the two distinct joint-eigenvalue labels used in the separated-range construction. For the swap of $2$ and $3$, $\rho=1-(-1)=2$ and $[2]_{-1}=0$, so the displayed separated-range generator formula is undefined here. [step 2.1, F1, F3]

4.1 Verify the failure of a JM-eigenbasis on this cell directly. Put $m_s=1+T_1$ and $m_t=(1+T_1)T_2$ modulo the higher row-shape ideal. The quadratic relation gives $m_sT_1=q m_s$. The higher row symmetrizer is $1+T_1+T_2+T_1T_2+T_2T_1+T_1T_2T_1$, so its vanishing in this cell gives $m_tT_1=-m_s-m_t$. At $q=-1$, since $L_2=q^{-1}T_1=-T_1$, it follows that $m_sL_2=m_s$ and $m_tL_2=m_s+m_t$. Thus $L_2-I$ is nonzero and $(L_2-I)^2=0$ on this two-dimensional cell. It is not diagonalizable over $\mathbb C$, so a simultaneous JM-eigenbasis cannot exist on this cell. Together with step 2.1 this supplies the claimed concrete boundary counterexample, without making a universal claim about all cells outside the separated range. [given, F2, step 3.1] ∎

before.statement: Let $R$ be an integral domain, $q\in R^{\times}$, $d,n\ge1$, and let $S(d,n)$ be the q-Schur algebra with Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Then $$G^{\lambda}_{\mu}=q^{N}\prod_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\\ b<c}}\left(\frac{[h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_q}{[h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_q}\right)^{d_{\mu}(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ab},\dots,\beta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots,\beta_n)},$$ where $N=N(\lambda,\mu)$ is the explicit integer $\sum_T\ell(d(\mathrm{last}(T)))$ summed over the semistandard $\lambda$-tableaux $T$ of type $\mu$ (the degree of the corresponding semistandard basis vector), $d_{\mu}$ is the signed semistandard multiplicity of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]] and $[\ \ ]_q$ are the quantum integers ([[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]). after.title: The q-Schur Weyl weight-space Gram determinant is a hook product
after.statement:
Let $R$ be an integral domain, $q\in R^\times$, $d,n\ge1$, and let $W^\lambda$ be the Weyl module of $S(d,n)$ for a partition $\lambda\vdash n$ with at most $d$ parts. For a composition $\mu$ of $n$ of length $d$, let $G^\lambda_\mu$ be the Gram determinant of its $\mu$-weight space in the semistandard basis ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Put $\beta_j=\lambda'_j+n-j$ and $h_{ab}=\lambda_a-b+\lambda'_b-a+1$. Then $$G^\lambda_\mu=q^N\prod_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\\b<c}}  \left(\frac{[h_{ab}]_q}{[h_{ac}]_q}\right)^{  d_\mu(\beta+h_{ac}\mathbf e_b-h_{ac}\mathbf e_c)},$$ where $N=\sum_{T\in T_0(\lambda,\mu)}\ell(d(\operatorname{last}(T)))$. Here $\operatorname{last}(T)$ is the least-dominant standardization in the fiber of $T$, and $d_\mu$ is the exact alternating semistandard number of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. **Both beta shifts use the same removed hook length $h_{ac}$.**

The exponent is the sorting sign times $|T_0(\eta,\mu)|$ if that balanced beta sequence has distinct nonnegative entries and recovers $\eta$; it is zero otherwise. Equivalently, remove the rim strip $R_{ac}$ and rewrap its $h_{ac}$ boxes with lowest node in column $b$. The sign is the parity of the heights of the removed strip and the newly added strip, the latter measured in the new diagram $\eta$; it is not generally the sum of two old $\lambda$ hook legs ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]], [[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]).

Form the product first in the universal field $\mathbb Q(Q)$. It equals a Laurent polynomial in $\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$, namely the universal integral Gram determinant divided by its displayed unit $Q^N$. Over $R$ the formula means the specialization of that Laurent polynomial. It does not require inverting a vanishing hook number or evaluating $0/0$. All weights and $d<n$ are retained; an empty weight space has determinant $1$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The normalized semistandard maps, weight projections and Weyl cell form of the q-Schur Definition; the beta symbols and branching identity; and the hook-to-bead-gap correspondence in the cited suppliers.

[F1] The ordinary cell maps have the normalization $\varphi_{ST}(m_\nu h)=m_{ST}h$, with $m_{ST}=\sum_{\mu(s)=S,\nu(t)=T}m_{st}$. Their star swaps the indices, and their four-index cell product defines the Weyl form ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). The actual regular corner identifies this product with the Murphy product with factor $1$ ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]).

[F2] Over $K=\mathbb Q(Q)$, the corrected intrinsic Murphy seminormal basis has its unitriangular normalization, adjacent-generator action and self-adjoint JM operators ([[thm-separated-hecke-residues-give-seminormal-idempotents-and-bases]]). For a semistandard $T$ and node $(i,j)$ of entry $v$, its predecessor set is precisely $$\Gamma_T(i,j)=\{(k,l):l<j,\ T(k,l)<v,\  T(k',l)>v\text{ for every }k'>k\}.$$ Equivalently $T(k,l)<v<T(k+1,l)$ with sentinel $+\infty$ below the column. Both inequalities are strict; an equal $v$ below excludes that column. Define $$\gamma_T:=\prod_{(i,j)}\prod_{(k,l)\in\Gamma_T(i,j)}  \frac{[j-i+k-l+1]_Q}{[j-i+k-l]_Q}.$$ The standard-tableau version is defined by the same rule.

[F3] The signed Kostka numbers satisfy $d_\mu(a)=\sum_{|C|=z}d_{\bar\mu}(a-\mathbf1_C)$, with zero values for repeated or negative beta entries ([[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Preserve small alphabets. Enlarge to $D=\max(d,n)$ temporarily. The sum of permutation summands with types supported on the first $d$ letters is a literal summand of the $D$-alphabet permutation module, with projection $p$ and $pS(D,n)p=S(d,n)$. The normalized maps whose two types have that support, their cell multiplication and their Weyl form coefficients are unchanged. Every semistandard shape with these types has at most $d$ rows. Thus proving the weight norm in the enlarged algebra, where the regular corner exists, proves the original norm as well. No hypothesis $d\ge n$ is added. [given, F1]

1.2 Compute the standard norms. For the canonical standard tableau, $\gamma_{t^\lambda}$ telescopes rowwise to $[\lambda]!_Q$, also its norm by $x_\lambda^2=[\lambda]!_Qx_\lambda$. If $s$ dominates $t=s(i,i+1)$, the adjacent action gives $f_t=f_s(T_i+\alpha)$ with $\alpha=1/[\rho]_Q$. Contravariance, orthogonality and the quadratic relation imply $\langle f_t,f_t\rangle=(Q+\alpha)(1-\alpha) \langle f_s,f_s\rangle$. The two swapped predecessor ratios give $\gamma_t=Q^{-1}(Q+\alpha)(1-\alpha)\gamma_s$: use $[\rho+1]=1+Q[\rho]$ and $[\rho-1]=Q^{-1}([\rho]-1)$. Increasing-length adjacent swaps of incomparable boxes reach every standard tableau, so $\langle f_t,f_t\rangle=Q^{\ell(d(t))}\gamma_t$. [F1, F2]

2.1 Compute the semistandard norms, including the missing scalar. Sums of JM elements over each label block commute with the corresponding row symmetrizer. Evaluation of the normalized map at $m_\mu$ gives their triangular action with leading eigenvalues $\sum_{T(i,j)=k}[j-i]_Q$. The joint eigenvalues distinguish $T$ over $K$: for every initial-label subshape they give its content multiset, whose diagonal counts determine the Young diagram. Finite triangular orthogonalization therefore gives $\psi_T=\varphi_T+$ more dominant terms. Let $U_T,V_T$ be the mutually adjoint cell maps between this weight and the regular weight, and let $\pi_t$ be the product of the axial ratios at standard predecessors with the **same** $T$-entry. Evaluation at $m_\mu$ gives $V_Tf_t=\pi_t\psi_T$: at the first standardization its scalar is the factorial of the row-intersection subgroup, also the telescoped $\pi_t$; an adjacent swap within a label block multiplies both scalars by $Q+\alpha$, since that row symmetrizer has $T_i$-eigenvalue $Q$. Finite bubble sorting connects the standardizations, proving the scalar for every $t$ in the fiber. For $t=\operatorname{last}(T)$, the strict boundary in [F2] partitions the standard predecessor set into $\Gamma_T$ and these same-entry predecessors, so $\gamma_t=\pi_t\gamma_T$. Also $U_T\psi_T$ has leading coefficient $1$ at $f_t$, all other terms more dominant, by the normalized map and the unitriangular basis changes. Hence adjointness gives $$\pi_t\langle\psi_T,\psi_T\rangle  =\langle f_t,U_T\psi_T\rangle  =Q^{\ell(d(t))}\gamma_t,$$ so $\langle\psi_T,\psi_T\rangle=Q^{\ell(d(t))}\gamma_T$. The transition determinant is $1$, yielding $G^\lambda_\mu=Q^N g^\lambda_\mu$ with $g^\lambda_\mu=\prod_T\gamma_T$. No norm is replaced by $Q^{\ell}$ alone. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 Prove the normalized beta product at the level of formal exponents. For $h\ge1$ put $$A_h(\beta,\mu)=-\sum_{b\ne c,\ \beta_b-h<\beta_c}  d_\mu(\beta-h\mathbf e_b+h\mathbf e_c).$$ A nonzero term requires $0\le\beta_b-h$, so the product is finite. Repeated beta entries cancel by exchanging the equal indices; a negative entry cannot become a valid term because, if it is the receiver, the lowered donor is still smaller. Thus these invalid sequences contribute zero exponents. Delete the largest semistandard label, occurring $z$ times in column feet $C$, to get $\beta-\mathbf1_C,\bar\mu$. The strict predecessor boundary excludes every column also in $C$. Consequently the literal exponent $E_h$ in $g$ obeys $$E_h(\beta,\mu)=\sum_{|C|=z}E_h(\beta-\mathbf1_C,\bar\mu)  +\sum_{|C|=z}\sum_{b\notin C,c\in C}  (\mathbf1_{\beta_b-\beta_c+1=h}-\mathbf1_{\beta_b-\beta_c=h})  d_{\bar\mu}(\beta-\mathbf1_C).$$ The final sum is exactly the axial ratio contributed by each deleted largest-label box. [F2, F3, step 2.1]

4.1 Verify the same recurrence for $A_h$. Apply [F3] to its summands and compare with $\sum_C A_h(\beta-\mathbf1_C,\bar\mu)$. Set $\delta=\beta_b-\beta_c-h$. The original condition is $\delta<0$ and the deleted one $\delta-\mathbf1_C(b)+\mathbf1_C(c)<0$. They differ only when $b\in C,c\notin C,\delta=0$ or $b\notin C,c\in C,\delta=-1$. In the first case, exchanging the two shifted beta entries turns the contribution into $-d_{\bar\mu}(\beta-\mathbf1_{C'})$ with $C'=C-b+c$, giving the negative term of step 3.1. In the second case, the exchanged entries give $+d_{\bar\mu}(\beta-\mathbf1_C)$, giving its positive term. Every other case cancels. At degree $0$ both exponent families vanish: a nonzero shifted empty beta sequence would have to exchange two entries with $h=\beta_b-\beta_c$, excluded by the strict condition. Induction gives $E_h=A_h$ and therefore $$g^\lambda_\mu=  \prod_{h\ge1}\prod_{b\ne c,\ \beta_b-h<\beta_c}  [h]_Q^{-d_\mu(\beta-h\mathbf e_b+h\mathbf e_c)}.$$ This proves the regrouping without copying the inconsistent signs in the printed display. [F3, step 3.1]

5.1 Convert to hooks. A surviving lowered bead $\beta_b-h$ is a nonnegative gap, so the bead-gap correspondence makes $h=h_{ab}$ for a node $(a,b)$. The remaining condition $\beta_c>\beta_b-h_{ab}=n-1-\lambda_a+a$ is equivalent to $c\le\lambda_a$; the paired nodes therefore lie in the same row. For $b<c$ write $h=h_{ab}$ and $k=h_{ac}$. Since $h-k=\beta_b-\beta_c$, the two ordered displaced sequences $\beta-h\mathbf e_b+h\mathbf e_c$ and $\beta-k\mathbf e_c+k\mathbf e_b$ exchange their two changed entries. Their signed numbers are negatives of each other, and their factors are exactly $([h]_Q/[k]_Q)^{d_\mu(\beta+k\mathbf e_b-k\mathbf e_c)}$. This proves the stated balanced hook product. Removing and rewrapping the $k$-strip is precisely this bead transfer; sorting counts its crossings, which are the heights of the removed and **new** strips. Colliding or negative sequences vanish by definition. [given, F3, step 4.1]

6.1 Specialize integrally. The semistandard form matrix has entries in $\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$, so its determinant and $Q^{-N}G^\lambda_\mu$ are Laurent polynomials. Steps 2.1-3.1 identify the rational products with these same polynomials in $\mathbb Q(Q)$. Base change of the free semistandard basis and its form now proves the identity over the given domain, including singular specializations and weights of dimension zero. No individual vanishing ratio is evaluated. All constructions are finite; no choice principle is used. [given, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1] ∎

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A PID $R$ with prime $\pi$, residue field $F$, $\hat q\in R^{\times}$ with $[n]!_{\hat q}\ne0$, the q-Schur algebra $S_F(d,n)$ and its Weyl modules with Jantzen filtrations ([[def-jantzen-filtration-of-a-lifted-cell-module]], [[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]), and the virtual Weyl and Specht symbols ([[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]).

[F1] ([[thm-q-schur-weyl-weight-space-gram-determinant-hook-product]]) The Gram determinant of $W^{\lambda}$ on its $\nu$-weight space equals $q^{N}$ times the hook-ratio product $\prod_{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda],b<c}([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q}/[h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q})^{d_{\mu}(\dots)}$; under $[n]!_{\hat q}\ne0$ every factor is nonzero in the domain $R$.

[F2] ([[lem-jantzen-layer-dimensions-equal-the-gram-determinant-valuation]]) The total dimension of the positive Jantzen layers on a non-degenerate form equals the $\pi$-adic valuation of its Gram determinant.

[F3] ([[lem-semistandard-weight-dimensions-detect-virtual-weyl-classes]]) Equality of all semistandard weight-space dimensions forces equality in the Grothendieck group of $S_F(d,n)$-modules.

[F4] The balanced displacement removes the $h_{ac}$-strip and adds the same number of boxes, preserving degree; its sign is the beta sorting sign ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]], [[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]).

[F5] The exact Schur functor has integral corner isomorphism and exact restricted form factor $1$, with $e^*=e$ ([[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]], [[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]). Filtration transport is proved below, rather than assumed from exactness.

[F6] Source results (Mathas, Theorem 5.31 and Corollary 5.32, printed pp. 58-60): the Jantzen sum formula for the q-Schur algebra and its transport to the Hecke side, with the coefficient $\nu_\pi([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q})-\nu_\pi([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q})$ and the virtual symbols.



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Work on a fixed weight space of the lifted free Weyl module. Every hook quantum integer is nonzero because its index is at most $n$ and $[n]!_{\hat q}\ne0$ in the domain. The balanced Gram formula [F1] gives its determinant, and the unit power of $\hat q$ has valuation zero. The Jantzen Gram-valuation lemma [F2] thus gives the sum of positive filtration-submodule dimensions as $$\sum_{(a,b),(a,c),\ b<c}  (\nu_\pi([h_{ab}]_{\hat q})-\nu_\pi([h_{ac}]_{\hat q}))  d_\mu(\beta+h_{ac}\mathbf e_b-h_{ac}\mathbf e_c).$$ The signed number is exactly the weight dimension of the corresponding balanced virtual Weyl symbol, including zero and cutoff cases. [given, F1, F2, F4]

2.1 Apply step 1.1 to every weight. The Weyl weight-character matrix is unitriangular, so [F3] detects equality of Grothendieck classes and proves part 1. These are classes of the filtration submodules $W_F^\lambda(i)$, not their successive quotients and not simply the radical class. [F3, step 1.1]

3.1 Establish filtration transport before applying the exact functor. On the lifted Weyl module $W$, the identity $e^*=e$ makes $We\perp W(1-e)$. For $x\in We$ and every $i\ge0$, pairing $x$ with all of $W$ is divisible by $\pi^i$ exactly when its pairing with $We$ is. Thus $W(i)e=(We)(i)$. Reducing modulo $\pi$ commutes with the direct summand projection, giving $W_F(i)e=(We)_F(i)$. The actual corner isomorphism and factor-$1$ form identity [F5] identify the latter with the Murphy Specht filtration. Applying the exact functor to the proved Weyl-class identity therefore transports each submodule and every signed term, proving part 2 even when a reduced cell form is identically zero. For the ordinary convention, apply the same $\theta$ to both modules and conjugate the labels; the independently proved Laurent-unit form factor preserves these divisibility filtrations as well. [F5, step 2.1]

4.1 Explain the valid multiplicity information. The Weyl form has nonzero simple head, $W_F(1)=\operatorname{rad}W_F$, and $W_F(i)\subseteq\operatorname{rad}W_F$ for $i>0$. Consequently for $\nu\ne\lambda$ its actual multiplicity in $W_F$ is its radical multiplicity, bounded above by its multiplicity in the whole positive sum. This whole-sum multiplicity is positive if and only if that factor occurs in the radical, since the first submodule is the radical and later ones lie inside it. ## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, parameter $q$, quantum characteristic $e$, integer $d\ge n$, and the Weyl modules in the statement. Write $S=S_F(d,n)$ and $W^{\lambda}=W^{\lambda}_F$.

[F1] The semistandard cellular basis has cells $W^{\lambda}$, nonzero absolutely simple heads $L^{\lambda}$, and dominance-unitriangular decomposition multiplicities $d_{\lambda\mu}$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). The cellular anti-involution induces contragredient duality fixing the simple isomorphism classes, through the nondegenerate cell form on each simple head ([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]], [[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]).

[F2] The balanced hook-ratio Jantzen formula and alternating beta symbols ([[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]], [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]) use conjugate beta numbers $\beta_j=\lambda'_j+N-j$, with $N$ sufficiently large, and read $$\sum_{r>0}[W^{\lambda}(r)]=\sum_{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda],\ b<c}\bigl(v(h^{\lambda}_{ab})-v(h^{\lambda}_{ac})\bigr)[W^{\beta+h^{\lambda}_{ac}\varepsilon_b-h^{\lambda}_{ac}\varepsilon_c}],$$ where $W^{\lambda}(r)$ are filtration submodules, $W^{\lambda}(1)=\operatorname{rad}W^{\lambda}$, and the right hand symbols are zero on repeated or negative entries and otherwise have the sign of sorting the beta sequence. The suppliers must carry this balanced form; the earlier displayed unbalanced manuscript indices do not preserve degree.

[F3] Core abaci are obtained by packing beads upwards on each runner, so their shapes depend only on runner bead counts; rim-hook removal is a bead-to-gap move ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]], [[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]], [[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]). Conjugation reverses dominance ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]).

[F4] Primitive central idempotents decompose the identity, and every finite-dimensional module splits into their block summands ([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]). Weyl classes are linearly independent in the Grothendieck group, so a nonzero accumulated Weyl coefficient in the class of a module supported in one block forces that Weyl module into the block ([[lem-virtual-weyl-combinations-detect-q-schur-block-separation]], [[lem-semistandard-weight-dimensions-detect-virtual-weyl-classes]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Lift and valuation. Use $R=F[X]_{(X-q)}$ with $\hat q=X$ and uniformizer $X-q$. The element $X$ is a unit since $q\ne0$, and every polynomial $[m]_X=1+X+\cdots+X^{m-1}$ is nonzero, so the generic factorial is nonzero. Its valuation $v(m)$ is positive exactly when $[m]_q=0$, equivalently $e\mid m$ for finite $e$; for $e=\infty$ all valuations vanish. In characteristic $p$ the positive valuation may exceed1, which causes no difficulty below. [given, F2, algebra]

1.2 Block support and Jantzen edges. A finite-dimensional module with simple head is indecomposable: every nonzero summand has nonzero head, so two summands would make the head nonsimple. Thus $W^{\lambda}$ has just one nonzero block summand, and every Jantzen submodule is supported in that block. By [F4], any nonzero accumulated coefficient $J_{\lambda\mu}$ of $[W^{\mu}]$ in [F2] puts $W^{\lambda},W^{\mu}$ in the same block. This uses the sum of submodule classes, without identifying it with the radical class. [F1, F2, F4]

2.1 Balanced terms preserve the core and descend in dominance. Put $s=h_{ab}$ and $t=h_{ac}$, so $s-t=\beta_b-\beta_c$. If a hook coefficient is nonzero, at least one of $s,t$ is divisible by $e$. If $e\mid t$, the shifted bead residues are unchanged. Otherwise $e\mid s$, so $t\equiv\beta_c-\beta_b\pmod e$ and the two shifted residues exchange. Thus every surviving symbol has the same runner counts and core as $\lambda$. Moreover replacing the two conjugate beta entries $u>v$ by $u+t,v-t$ strictly increases conjugate majorization; the sorted target therefore strictly decreases original dominance. Accumulating equal target labels preserves both conclusions. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 No outgoing edge implies a binary row condition. Suppose every accumulated outgoing coefficient from $\mu$ is zero. For row $i$, put $g_i=N+i-1-\mu_i$, a gap in its conjugate beta set; its row hooks are exactly $\beta_j-g_i>0$. If that row contained a divisible hook $s$ and a nondivisible hook $t$, repeatedly replace $t$ by $s+t$ while their sum is another row hook. This finite climb ends with $s+t$ absent from the hook set. The balanced term for the nodes of hook lengths $s,t$ then has lower shifted bead $g_i$, which is a gap, and upper shifted bead $g_i+s+t$, which is absent from the beta set. Its symbol survives and its coefficient is $\pm v(s)\ne0$. There is no cancellation: any surviving balanced term replaces two lost values by a new value larger than both and a new value smaller than both, so those four values determine the pair and its row gap uniquely; the gaps $g_i$ strictly increase with $i$. This contradicts the zero accumulated coefficient. Therefore each row has either all hook lengths divisible by $e$ or none; call this the binary row condition. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Composition-factor cores. An off-head simple occurs in $W^{\lambda}$ exactly when it occurs in its radical, equivalently in the positive Jantzen sum: the first submodule is the radical and every later one is contained in it. Its nonzero multiplicity in that sum implies it occurs in some $W^{\mu}$ with $J_{\lambda\mu}\ne0$, since otherwise its coefficient in the sum would be zero. Step 2.1 gives the same core and strict dominance descent. Induction on the finite dominance poset proves that every factor $L^{\nu}$ of $W^{\lambda}$ has $C_e(\nu)=C_e(\lambda)$. No identity equating the radical class with the positive sum is asserted. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 Vertical core removal under the binary row condition. A removable $e$-hook has hook length $e$ at its defining node. Every hook in that row is then divisible, so its last-column hook, a positive multiple of $e$ no larger than $e$, equals $e$. Hook lengths strictly decrease across the row, forcing the defining node to be at the row end: the strip is vertical on $e$ equal-length rows $i,\ldots,i+e-1$ in column $j$. Removing it decreases that column height by $e$. In unaffected rows hook divisibility is unchanged. For an affected row $i+t$, hooks in the retained columns were all congruent to $-t$ modulo $e$, because row $i$ had all hooks divisible and those rows had equal length. Their new hook lengths are all congruent to $-t-1$, so the binary row condition persists. Induction shows every core-removal strip is vertical. [F3, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 The Cartan graph locally. Choose a complete orthogonal primitive idempotent system of $S$, with one representative $f_\mu$ for each simple label and repeated representatives as necessary. Such a system lifts matrix diagonal idempotents from the split semisimple quotient: the radical is nilpotent and the iteration $u\mapsto u+(1-2u)(u^2-u)$ squares the idempotency error, so finite iteration lifts an idempotent; successively working in complementary corners lifts an orthogonal system. Absolute simplicity gives $\dim L^{\lambda}f_\mu=\delta_{\lambda\mu}$, hence exact multiplication by $f_\mu$ gives $\dim W^{\lambda}f_\mu=d_{\lambda\mu}$. The successive cellular ideal bimodules are the contragredient cell module tensor the right cell module. Apply the exact projection $f_\mu(-)f_\nu$ and add their dimensions; [F1]'s duality fixes the simple labels, giving $\dim f_\mu Sf_\nu=\sum_\lambda d_{\lambda\mu}d_{\lambda\nu}$. This is the Cartan entry of the primitive projective $f_\mu S$. A disconnected graph on the full primitive idempotent system, with edges whenever either mixed corner is nonzero, yields central idempotents by summing each component: all mixed corners vanish in both directions. Conversely a central block idempotent forbids mixed corners. Thus simple labels in one block are joined by pairs sharing a Weyl factor, and step 3.1 proves that labels in the same block have the same core. [F1, F4, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 The minimum label and the bridge shapes. Fix core $\gamma$ and weight $w$, and set $\rho=(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_l,1^{ew})$. It has core $\gamma$ by removing its bottom vertical $e$-strips, and is dominance-minimal in the class: every same-core partition contains $\gamma$ as a diagram, and appending all additional boxes as rows of size1 minimizes each dominance partial sum. Let $\mu\ne\rho$ satisfy the binary row condition. Choose the first row $i$ with divisible hooks and put $j=\mu_i$, $h=h^{\mu}_{ij}=\mu'_j-i+1$, a positive multiple of $e$. If $j=1$, every divisible hook is in column1, so step 3.2 would give $\mu=\rho$; thus $j>1$. Remove the vertical $h$-strip, obtaining $\sigma$, then add $h$ boxes horizontally to its first row to get $\nu$, and vertically to its first column to get $\eta$. All have the same core, since $h$ is a multiple of $e$; $\nu$ dominates $\mu,\eta$, and $\eta$ is strictly below $\mu$ because the removed nodes are moved into new bottom rows. [F3, step 3.2, construct, algebra]

5.1 The bridge coefficients are nonzero. Write $l=\ell(\mu)=\ell(\sigma)$. If $i>1$, then $\sigma_1=\mu_1$ and the row1 hook pair in $\nu$ at columns $j,\mu_1+1$ has lengths $A=h^{\mu}_{1j}$ and $h$: the first is nondivisible because row1 precedes the first divisible row, and the second is divisible. Its balanced symbol sorts to $\mu$, so its coefficient is nonzero. If $i=1$, then $\sigma_1=j-1$, and the row1 pair at columns $j,j+1$ has lengths $h,h-1$; its balanced transfer $h-1$ sorts to $\mu$, again giving a nonzero coefficient. For $\eta$, the pair at columns $1,\sigma_1+1$ has lengths $A'=\sigma_1+h+l-1$ and $h$. When $i>1$, $A'-h^{\mu}_{i1}=A$, so $A'$ is nondivisible; when $i=1$, $A'=h^{\mu}_{11}+h-1$, also nondivisible. Its balanced symbol sorts to $\eta$. Each claimed target has precisely two lost and two gained beta values, so the uniqueness argument in step 2.2 rules out cancellation. Thus both $J_{\nu\mu}$ and $J_{\nu\eta}$ are nonzero. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.2, step 4.2, algebra]

6.1 Connectivity and sufficiency. Induct upwards from $\rho$ in the finite dominance poset. For $\mu\ne\rho$, if an outgoing coefficient $J_{\mu\tau}$ is nonzero, then $\tau$ is strictly below $\mu$ in the same core class by step 2.1, so induction connects $\tau$, and hence $\mu$, to $\rho$. If no outgoing coefficient exists, steps 2.2, 3.2, 4.2 and 5.1 connect $\mu$ to $\nu$ and then $\eta$, with $\eta$ strictly below $\mu$, and induction again connects it to $\rho$. Every such edge is a same-block implication by step 1.2. Thus every pair of labels of the same core lies in the same block. Together with step 4.1 this proves the equivalence. [step 1.2, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 2.2, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Parameterization and infinite characteristic. Every simple is the head of a Weyl module, so every block has a partition label. The core sizes are $n-ew$, and each admissible core occurs via the partition $\rho$ of step 4.2; step 6.1 therefore gives the stated indexing. If $e=\infty$, all coefficients vanish by step 1.1, so positivity forces every first Jantzen submodule, hence every radical, to vanish. All Weyl modules are simple; their decomposition matrix is the identity. Step 4.1 then gives identity Cartan matrix, so every primitive projective is simple and $S$ is semisimple, with each partition its own block and core. This proves all assertions. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 6.1] ∎

The connectivity argument follows the corrected dominance-minimum route of Lyle–Mathas Proposition 3.7 and Corollary 4.3, while proving the needed elementary row properties locally. Their final Remark explicitly corrects the earlier first-row-only q-Schur argument; the old direct hook move can have zero coefficient.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e$, a partition $n\ge0$, the Hecke algebra $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ with Specht modules $S^{\lambda}$ for $\lambda\vdash n$, and a fixed integer $d\ge n$.

[F1] For $d\ge n$, the Schur idempotent $e\in S=S_F(d,n)$ satisfies $eSe\cong H$, and $X\mapsto Xe$ is exact. It sends each Weyl module $W^{\lambda}$ to the nonzero Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$; its simple images are zero or the Murphy simple modules, with the nonzero images indexed by the $e$-restricted partitions ([[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]], [[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]).

[F2] Blocks: $1=\sum_D\delta_D$ is the unique decomposition of the identity of a finite-dimensional algebra into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents, blocks are the ideals cut out by the $\delta_D$, and every nonzero central idempotent is a sum of some of the $\delta_D$ ([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]], [[lem-the-identity-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-decomposes-into-primitive-central-idempotents]], [[lem-central-idempotent-decompositions-of-one-are-unique]]).

[F3] The q-Schur algebra and its Weyl modules: $S$ is finite-dimensional, $S=\mathrm{End}_H(M)$ for $M=\bigoplus_{\nu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\nu}$ with $M^{(1^n)}=H$, and $W^{\lambda}_F$ has head $L^{\lambda}_F$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]).

[F4] The q-Schur block theorem [[thm-q-schur-weyl-modules-are-in-the-same-block-iff-their-labels-have-the-same-e-core]]: for $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$, the Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}_F,W^{\mu}_F$ lie in the same block of $S$ if and only if $C_e(\lambda)=C_e(\mu)$; the blocks of $S$ are indexed by the $e$-cores $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n$, $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$; and if $e=\infty$ then $S$ is semisimple with each $W^{\lambda}_F$ its own block.

[F5] The accepted ordinary/Murphy dictionary identifies the ordinary Specht module with the fixed $\theta$ pullback of the conjugate-shape Murphy cell module. Conjugation sends $C_e(\lambda)$ to $C_e(\lambda)'$, and sends restricted labels to regular labels. In particular it preserves equality of cores. An algebra automorphism permutes primitive central idempotents and therefore preserves the same-block relation ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Central idempotents of $H$ from blocks of $S$. For a block $C$ of $S$ with primitive central idempotent $\epsilon_C$ put $\tilde\epsilon_C:=\epsilon_Ce=e\epsilon_Ce\in H$. This element is a central idempotent of $H$: it is idempotent because $\epsilon_C$ is, and for $x=ese\in H$ centrality of $\epsilon_C$ gives $x\tilde\epsilon_C=es\epsilon_Ce=e\epsilon_Cse=\tilde\epsilon_Cx$; it is nonzero because it acts as the identity on the nonzero module $W^{\lambda}_Fe=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ for any $\lambda$ with $W^{\lambda}_F\in C$, namely $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\tilde\epsilon_C=W^{\lambda}_Fe\epsilon_Ce=W^{\lambda}_F\epsilon_Ce=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$. Moreover $\tilde\epsilon_C\tilde\epsilon_{C'}=e\epsilon_C\epsilon_{C'}e=0$ for $C\ne C'$ and $\sum_C\tilde\epsilon_C=e\sum_C\epsilon_Ce=e^2=1_H$. [F1, F2, F3]

1.2 Number of q-Schur blocks is at least the number of Hecke blocks. Let $H=\bigoplus_iB_i$ be the block decomposition of $H$ with block identities $b_i$. Since $M=\bigoplus_{\nu}M^{\nu}$ and $H=M^{(1^n)}$ is a direct summand, $M=\bigoplus_iMb_i$ with each $Mb_i\ne0$ (it contains $Hb_i=B_i$), and $\mathrm{Hom}_H(Mb_i,Mb_j)=0$ for $i\ne j$, because a map $f$ satisfies $f(x)=f(xb_i)=f(x)b_i\in Mb_jb_i=0$. Hence $$S=\mathrm{End}_H(M)=\bigoplus_{i,j}\mathrm{Hom}_H(Mb_i,Mb_j)=\prod_i\mathrm{End}_H(Mb_i)$$ is a product of the nonzero algebras $\mathrm{End}_H(Mb_i)$, and a product of nonzero algebras has at least one block per factor; so $\#\{\text{blocks of }S\}\ge\#\{\text{blocks of }H\}$. [F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Number of Hecke blocks is at least the number of q-Schur blocks. Decompose each nonzero central idempotent $\tilde\epsilon_C$ of step 1.1 into primitive central idempotents of $H$ using the unique decomposition of $1_H$: every primitive central idempotent $\delta_D$ of $H$ with $\delta_D\tilde\epsilon_C=\delta_D$ belongs to exactly one $\tilde\epsilon_C$, because $\delta_D=\delta_D\cdot1_H=\sum_C\delta_D\tilde\epsilon_C$ and pairwise orthogonality of the $\delta_D$ forces $\delta_D\tilde\epsilon_C\in\{0,\delta_D\}$. Since each $\tilde\epsilon_C\ne0$ has at least one such $\delta_D$, the blocks $D$ of $H$ are partitioned into nonempty supports over the blocks $C$ of $S$, and therefore $\#\{\text{blocks of }H\}\ge\#\{\text{blocks of }S\}$. [F2, step 1.1]

3.1 A bijection of block sets, and the core criterion. By steps 2.1 and 1.2 the two block counts are equal, so each $\tilde\epsilon_C$ of step 1.1 has exactly one primitive summand and the map $C\mapsto\tilde\epsilon_C$ is a bijection from the blocks of $S$ onto the blocks of $H$. Since $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}=W^{\lambda}_Fe$ and $S^{\mu}_{\mathrm M}=W^{\mu}_Fe$, the modules $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ and $S^{\mu}_{\mathrm M}$ lie in the same Hecke block if and only if $W^{\lambda}_F$ and $W^{\mu}_F$ lie in the same q-Schur block: indeed the block of $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is the image under the bijection of the block of $W^{\lambda}_F$. By the block theorem [F4] the latter holds if and only if $C_e(\lambda)=C_e(\mu)$, which proves the q-Schur-normalised statement. [F1, F4, step 2.1, step 1.2]

4.1 Ordinary normalisation and semisimplicity. By [F5], $S^{\lambda}$ and $S^{\mu}$ lie in the same block exactly when $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$ and $S^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}$ do. Step 3.1 makes this equivalent to $C_e(\lambda')=C_e(\mu')$, and the identity $C_e(\nu')=C_e(\nu)'$ makes it equivalent to $C_e(\lambda)=C_e(\mu)$. This identity follows by conjugating every removable border strip in a core-removal sequence; the terminal core also conjugates, by independence of removal order. For $e=\infty$, $S$ is semisimple by [F4]. Its corner $eSe$ is semisimple: in the Wedderburn decomposition of $S$, each idempotent selects a subspace in each matrix factor, and its corner is a product of matrix algebras over the same division rings. Thus $H\cong eSe$ is semisimple; the block bijection separates the partition labels. This proves all assertions. [F1, F4, F5, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

before.statement: Let $k$ be a splitting field of characteristic $p>0$ (equivalently the residue field of the fixed splitting $p$-modular system, [[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]], [[def-p-blocks-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]) and let $n\ge0$. Two Specht modules $S^{\lambda}_k,S^{\mu}_k$ of $k[S_n]$ lie in the same block of $k[S_n]$ if and only if $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ have the same $p$-core ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]).
