## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A splitting field $k$ of characteristic $p>0$ with the fixed splitting $p$-modular system, an integer $n\ge0$, and the group algebra $k[S_n]$ with group Specht modules $S^{\lambda}_k$ for $\lambda\vdash n$.

[F1] The algebra isomorphism $H_{k,1}(S_n)\cong k[S_n]$ sends each ordinary Dipper-James Specht module to the classical group Specht module of the same shape, and the quantum characteristic at $q=1$ in characteristic $p$ equals $p$ ([[prop-hecke-specht-theory-specializes-to-group-specht-theory-at-q-one]], [[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]). The module comparison uses the accepted signed conjugate Murphy/ordinary dictionary before specialising; it does not identify the same-shape Murphy cell module with the ordinary Specht module.

[F2] The Hecke block criterion, in the Dipper-James normalisation of the same Specht modules as [F1]: [[cor-type-a-hecke-specht-modules-are-in-the-same-block-iff-their-labels-have-the-same-e-core]] states that for a field $k$ and $q\in k^{\times}$ of quantum characteristic $e\ge2$, two Specht modules $S^{\lambda},S^{\mu}$ of $H_{k,q}(S_n)$ lie in the same block if and only if $C_e(\lambda)=C_e(\mu)$, and that the blocks are indexed by the $e$-cores $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n$ and $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$.

[F4] The core-quotient size formula [[prop-core-quotient-size-and-weight-formula]]: for every $e\ge2$ and $\lambda\vdash n$ one has $n=|C_e(\lambda)|+e\,w_e(\lambda)$ with $w_e(\lambda)=|Q_e(\lambda)|\in\mathbb N_0$, and for an $e$-core $\gamma$ the condition $|\gamma|\le n$, $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$ is exactly the condition that $n-|\gamma|$ be an admissible $e$-weight; conversely every such $\gamma$ occurs as the core of a partition of $n$ ([[thm-q-schur-weyl-modules-are-in-the-same-block-iff-their-labels-have-the-same-e-core]], [[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]]).

[F5] An algebra isomorphism $\varphi:A\to B$ preserves blocks: it maps a central idempotent $z$ to the central idempotent $\varphi(z)$, preserves primitivity, and hence induces a bijection between the block sets ([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]], [[lem-central-idempotent-decompositions-of-one-are-unique]]).

## Proof

 **Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Specialisation. Take $q=1\in k^{\times}$ and $e$ the quantum characteristic of $(k,q)$; since $q=1$ and $\operatorname{char}k=p>0$, [F1] gives $e=p$. By [F1] there is an algebra isomorphism $H_{k,1}(S_n)\cong k[S_n]$ carrying the Hecke Specht modules of $H_{k,1}(S_n)$ to the group Specht modules $S^{\lambda}_k$, so by [F5] this isomorphism induces a bijection between the blocks of the two algebras that matches $S^{\lambda}$ with $S^{\lambda}_k$; in particular $S^{\lambda}_k$ and $S^{\mu}_k$ lie in the same block of $k[S_n]$ if and only if the corresponding Hecke Specht modules lie in the same block of $H_{k,1}(S_n)$. [F1, F5, algebra]

2.1 The core criterion. Applying the Hecke block criterion [F2] with $q=1$ and $e=p$, the Hecke Specht modules of $H_{k,1}(S_n)$ lie in the same block if and only if the labels $\lambda,\mu$ have the same $p$-core. Together with step 1.1 this gives: $S^{\lambda}_k$ and $S^{\mu}_k$ lie in the same block of $k[S_n]$ if and only if $C_p(\lambda)=C_p(\mu)$. [F2, step 1.1]

3.1 The parametrisation by cores and weights. By [F2] the blocks of $H_{k,1}(S_n)$, hence by step 1.1 the blocks of $k[S_n]$, are indexed by the $p$-cores $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n$ and $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod p$; the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ corresponds to $C_p(\lambda)$. For $n\ge0$ and such a $\gamma$ put $w:=(n-|\gamma|)/p\in\mathbb N_0$; by [F4] this is exactly the $p$-weight $w_p(\lambda)$ of any Specht label with core $\gamma$, and $n=|\gamma|+pw$. Since $w$ is determined by $n$ and $\gamma$, the map $\gamma\mapsto(\gamma,w)$ is a bijection onto the displayed set of pairs, and the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ is the pair $(C_p(\lambda),w_p(\lambda))$. [F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Steps 2.1 and 3.1 establish both assertions: the same-block criterion by the $p$-core, and the indexing of the blocks by the pairs $(\gamma,w)$ with $n=|\gamma|+pw$ together with the identification of the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ as $(C_p(\lambda),w_p(\lambda))$. [step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

The classification is stated independently, by a Young-module and Brauer-quotient route, as Theorem 1 of O'Donovan's preprint recorded in the sources; that reference is an independent confirmation of the statement and is not used in the proof above. No choice principle is used anywhere in this item.

before.title: Cellularity does not make every cell module simple
before.statement: A cellular algebra need not be semisimple, its cell modules need not be simple, and a labelled cell-form quotient $D^{\lambda}$ may vanish although the cell module $C^{\lambda}$ is nonzero. (a) Abstract degenerate instance: let $F$ be a field and $A=F[x]/(x^2)$, with $\Lambda=\{2\rhd1\}$ ordered so that $2\rhd1$, cellular basis $c_{11}:=1$ in cell $1$ and $c_{22}:=x$ in cell $2$ and $i=\mathrm{id}$ ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For $a+bx\in A$ one has $1(a+bx)\equiv a\cdot1\pmod{(x)}$ and $x(a+bx)=ax$, so the triangular axiom holds, and $A^{\rhd1}=(x)$, $A^{\rhd2}=0$. The cell form on $C^{2}$ has $c_{22}c_{22}=x^2=0$, so it is identically zero, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{2}=C^{2}$ and $D^{2}=0$, while both $C^{1}$ and $C^{2}$ are one-dimensional simple modules: on either, $a+bx$ acts as the scalar $a$. In particular the Jacobson radical of $C^{2}$ is zero and its actual head is $C^{2}$, even though its cell-form radical is all of $C^{2}$ and its cell-form quotient is zero: cellularity does not force $D^{\lambda}\ne0$, and the algebra is not semisimple since $\mathrm{rad}\,A=(x)$. (b) Hecke instance: let $F$ be a field of characteristic $2$ and $q=1$, so $e=\operatorname{char}(F)=2$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]); for $n=3$ and $\lambda=(1,1,1)$ the partition $(1,1,1)$ is not $2$-regular ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]), so $D^{(1,1,1)}=0$ while the page's Specht module $S^{(1,1,1)}\cong D^{(3)}$ is the nonzero trivial module (in characteristic $2$ the sign module is trivial) ([[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]], [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]). (c) Reducible cell module: at $e=2$ the q-Schur cell module $W^{(3,2)}_F$ satisfies $\sum_{i>0}[W^{(3,2)}_F(i)]=[L^{(3,1^2)}_F]+2[L^{(2^2,1)}_F]\ne0$ ([[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]], the calculation of [[ex-q-schaper-for-shape-three-two-at-e-two]]), so its radical is nonzero and $W^{(3,2)}_F$ is reducible even though it has a simple head.
before.strategy: Part (a) is a direct computation in the two-dimensional algebra $F[x]/(x^2)$: every product of two elements of the smaller cell vanishes. Part (b) reads the $2$-regularity of $(1,1,1)$ off the definition and applies the classification theorem; the cell module $S^{(1^3)}$ at $q=1$ is the sign module, which is the trivial module in characteristic $2$. Part (c) is the Weyl-module computation of Example 5.33, where the Jantzen layers have positive dimension. All three instances are applications of [[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]], whose third clause says that $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ holds exactly when the cell form is not identically zero, and identifies the form radical with the module Jacobson radical only in that nonzero-quotient case. No choice is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The three settings above: the algebra $A=F[x]/(x^2)$, the Hecke algebra $H_{F,q}(S_3)$ in characteristic $2$ at $q=1$, and the q-Schur Weyl module $W^{(3,2)}_F$ over $F=\mathbb C$, $q=-1$, at $e=2$.

[F1] ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]], [[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]) For a cellular basis, products of two elements of the smaller cell vanish modulo the larger cell exactly when the corresponding form entry vanishes; $D^{\lambda}=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is zero if and only if the cell form is identically zero, and only in the nonzero case is $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ the module-theoretic Jacobson radical and the head quotient.

[F2] ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]], [[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]) For $F$ of characteristic $2$ and $q=1$ the quantum characteristic is $e=2$, $(1,1,1)$ is not $2$-regular, and $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ exactly for the $e$-regular $\lambda$.

[F3] ([[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]], [[ex-q-schaper-for-shape-three-two-at-e-two]]) For the specified $F=\mathbb C$, $q=-1$ lift with $e=2$, the positive Jantzen submodule sum for $W^{(3,2)}_F$ is $[L^{(3,1^2)}_F]+2[L^{(2^2,1)}_F]\ne0$.




## Counterexample

1.1 The abstract instance: in $A=F[x]/(x^2)$ with $c_{11}=1$, $c_{22}=x$ and $2\rhd1$, the product $c_{22}c_{22}=x^2=0$ is congruent to $0\cdot c_{22}$ modulo $A^{\rhd2}=0$, so the axiom holds with zero form value; the products $c_{11}(a+bx)=a+bx\equiv a\,c_{11}\pmod{(x)}$ and $c_{22}(a+bx)=ax=a\,c_{22}$ confirm the triangularity. Hence $C^{2}$ has identically zero form, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{2}=C^{2}$ and $D^{2}=0$; the module $C^{2}$ itself is one-dimensional with $a+bx$ acting as $a$, hence simple with zero Jacobson radical and head $C^{2}\ne0$. Moreover $x\in A$ is a nonzero nilpotent, so $\mathrm{rad}\,A=(x)\ne0$ and $A$ is not semisimple. [given, F1]

1.2 The Hecke instance: for $F$ of characteristic $2$ and $q=1$ the sign module is the trivial module, so the Murphy cell module $S^{(3)}_{\mathrm M}$ and its theta-pullback $S^{(1,1,1)}=(S^{(3)}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$ are the trivial module; the label $(1,1,1)$ is not $2$-regular, so by [F2] $D^{(1,1,1)}=0$ while $S^{(1,1,1)}\ne0$. [given, F2]

1.3 The reducible Weyl module. In the precise lift of [F3], the sum of the positive filtration-submodule classes is $[L^{(3,1^2)}]+2[L^{(2,2,1)}]\ne0$. At least one of these submodules is nonzero. Since all are contained in the first reduced submodule $W_F(1)=\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}W_F$, that radical is nonzero. The Schur cell form has nonzero simple head, so its form radical is its unique maximal proper submodule. Consequently $W_F^{(3,2)}$ is reducible, despite having simple head $L^{(3,2)}$. The reduced form radical is not identified with $F\otimes_R$ the generic radical: specialization need not commute with this kernel, and the lifted generic form here is nondegenerate. [given, F1, F3]

2.1 Conclusion: the three instances refute the claims that cellularity forces semisimplicity, forces every cell module to be simple, or forces every labelled cell-form quotient to be nonzero; each is an application of the classification of cell-form quotients [F1] together with the explicit degenerate data. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, F1] ∎
